# How Many Questions Are on the SAT? 2026: What to Know


## TL;DR


The Digital SAT has 98 questions total: 54 Reading and Writing questions and 44 Math questions. The test is divided into four separately timed modules and takes 2 hours and 14 minutes of testing time, plus a 10-minute break. Eight questions are unscored pretest questions, leaving 90 operational questions that contribute to scoring. However, the SAT does not use a simple percentage-correct system: scores are calculated using an adaptive scoring model that considers the difficulty and characteristics of the questions you answer.


[Take a free SAT practice test](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-tests) to see these 98 questions in action before reading further.


## How Many Questions Are on the SAT?


The Digital SAT has **98 questions total** : 54 Reading and Writing questions and 44 Math questions. Each section is divided into two modules, giving you 27 Reading and Writing questions per module and 22 Math questions per module. You have 64 minutes for Reading and Writing and 70 minutes for Math, for 2 hours and 14 minutes of testing time overall.

Each SAT section has two separately timed modules. Reading and Writing gives you 32 minutes per module, while Math gives you 35 minutes per module. You cannot transfer unused time from one module to another, and you cannot return to a previous module after its time expires.


## How Many Questions Are on SAT Math?


The SAT Math section has **44 questions** , divided evenly between two 35-minute modules. Each Math module contains 22 questions. Approximately 75% of Math questions use four-option multiple choice, while about 25% use student-produced response, where you enter the answer yourself.

## How Many SAT Questions Actually Count Toward Your Score?

The important catch is that you **cannot identify the pretest questions** while taking the SAT. They are designed to look like regular test questions, so you should treat all 98 questions as if they count.


Also, do not think of the SAT as a simple 90-question percentage test. College Board uses an adaptive scoring model based on Item Response Theory, so two students who answer the same number of questions correctly can receive different section scores depending on the questions they answered.


One practical takeaway worth remembering: if you’re stuck on a particularly strange question, there’s a real chance it’s one of the 8 pretest items. Flag it, move on, and come back if time allows. Understanding[how the Digital SAT is scored](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-is-the-digital-sat-scored-adaptive-scoring) will help you make smarter decisions about where to spend your time.


## Can You Tell Which SAT Questions Are Experimental?


No. The 8 pretest questions are embedded throughout the SAT and are not identified for students. They are designed to look like operational questions so College Board can collect performance data on potential future test questions.


For that reason, do not skip a question because it seems unusually difficult, unfamiliar, or strangely worded. It could be an unscored pretest item, but there is no reliable way to know. The safest strategy is to give every question your best effort.


## What Types of Questions Appear on the SAT?


Knowing how many questions are on the SAT matters more when you understand what those questions look like.


**Reading and Writing:** All 54 questions are standard multiple-choice with four answer options. Each question is paired with a short passage (typically one paragraph), which is a significant change from the old SAT’s long multi-paragraph reading passages.


**Math:** The 44 Math questions come in two formats. Roughly 75% (about 33 questions) are traditional multiple-choice with four options. The remaining 25% (about 11 questions) are student-produced response, or SPR, where you type in a numeric answer rather than selecting from choices. SPR questions demand more precision because there are no answer choices to eliminate or back-solve from.


Both sections use rights-only scoring. Every correct answer earns one point. Wrong answers and blank answers both earn zero. There is no guessing penalty, so you should always answer every single question, even if you’re guessing blindly. A random guess has a 25% chance of being correct on multiple-choice items. Leaving it blank has a 0% chance.


Want to get a feel for both question formats?[Try free SAT practice questions](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-questions) to see the difference between multiple-choice and student-produced response firsthand.

## How the Adaptive System Affects Your Questions


The Digital SAT uses a multistage adaptive testing design. This is the feature that confuses students the most, so here’s a clean explanation.


Each section (Reading and Writing, Math) has two modules. Module 1 is the same difficulty mix for everyone, a spread of easy, medium, and hard questions. Your performance on Module 1 determines whether Module 2 is generally harder or generally easier.


A strong performance on Module 1 can route you to a second module with a higher difficulty mix, while a weaker performance can route you to a lower-difficulty mix. The goal is not simply to get the “hard” module. Your final section score is based on your performance across both modules and the characteristics of the questions you answered.


This is why Module 1 matters: it helps determine the difficulty mix you will see in Module 2. However, you should not deliberately try to miss questions to manipulate your route. College Board's research indicates that students are best served by answering every question to the best of their ability.


Practitioners in SAT tutoring communities consistently emphasize that Module 1 is the highest-leverage moment of the entire test. A student who rushes Module 1 and gets sloppy gets punished twice: lower direct points from careless errors, and a capped second module they can never catch up from. The strategic implication is clear. Slow down slightly on Module 1 and prioritize accuracy over speed.


If you’re unsure where your Module 1 performance would land you,[start with a diagnostic](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/digital-sat-prep) to identify your current level before building a study plan.

The SAT went from 154 questions to 98, a reduction of 56 questions and 46 minutes. This wasn’t about making the test easier. Adaptive testing technology allows College Board to measure the same skills more efficiently. Each question now carries more scoring weight, and the adaptive routing provides precise measurement without needing as many items.


One change worth highlighting: a calculator is now permitted on every math question, with a built-in Desmos graphing calculator available in the test interface. The old “No Calculator” math section is gone entirely.

## Can You Go Back to SAT Questions?


Yes, you can move between questions and change your answers while a module is still active. You can also flag questions to revisit later in that same module.


However, once a module's time expires and the test moves forward, you cannot return to that module. Because each module is separately timed, unused time does not carry over to the next module.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Does every SAT administration have the same number of questions?


Yes. Every Digital SAT has exactly 98 questions: 54 Reading and Writing and 44 Math, arranged in four modules. The adaptive system changes the difficulty of Module 2, not the question count.


### Can I skip questions and go back to them?


You can move freely within a single module, flagging questions to revisit before time runs out. You cannot go back to a previous module once it’s finished.


### Is there a penalty for guessing on the SAT?


No. The SAT uses rights-only scoring. Wrong answers are worth exactly the same as blank answers: zero points. Always guess if you can’t solve the problem.


### How many questions do I need to get right for a 1500?


The exact number depends on the difficulty of your specific test form and which adaptive module you’re routed to. As a rough benchmark, you’ll need to get the vast majority of your 90 scored questions correct. A[score predictor](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/score-predictors) can give you a more precise estimate based on your practice performance.


### How many SAT Math questions are multiple-choice vs. fill-in?


About 33 of the 44 Math questions (75%) are standard four-option multiple-choice. The remaining 11 or so (25%) are student-produced response questions where you type in a numeric answer.


### What’s the scoring range for the SAT?


Total scores range from 400 to 1600. Each section (Reading and Writing, Math) is scored on a scale of 200 to 800, and those two section scores are added together. For context on where different scores land, check out this[guide to good SAT scores](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/what-is-a-good-sat-score-guide) .


### How long should I study for the SAT?


That depends on your starting score and target. Most students benefit from 2-4 months of focused preparation. Read more about[how long to study for the SAT](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-long-to-study-for-sat-hours-timelines) for specific hour recommendations based on your score gap.


### Can I use a calculator on the entire Math section?


Yes. Unlike the old paper SAT, which had a no-calculator math section, the Digital SAT allows calculator use on all 44 Math questions. A Desmos graphing calculator is built into the testing interface, or you can bring your own approved calculator.


### How Many SAT Questions Do You Need to Get Right for a 1500?


There is no fixed number of correct answers that guarantees a 1500 on the Digital SAT. The SAT uses an adaptive scoring model that considers the difficulty and characteristics of the questions you answer, so two students with the same number of correct answers can receive different scores.


For that reason, do not use a simple “X out of 90” formula to predict a 1500. The most reliable way to estimate your performance is to take an official full-length adaptive practice test in Bluebook under realistic testing conditions and review your section scores and missed questions. College Board says its full-length practice tests are highly indicative of actual SAT performance when taken under similar conditions.


### Is the Digital SAT Easier Because It Has Fewer Questions?


Not necessarily. The Digital SAT has fewer questions and less testing time than the old SAT, but it uses multistage adaptive testing and Item Response Theory to measure students' skills with fewer items. The difficulty and structure of the test are therefore different from the old paper SAT rather than simply being a shorter version of it.


### How Many Questions Are on Each SAT Module?


The Reading and Writing modules each contain 27 questions, while the Math modules each contain 22 questions. That means the SAT has 49 questions in its first two modules and 49 questions in its second two modules, for 98 questions total. Each module is separately timed.


### Are SAT Questions Multiple Choice?


Most SAT questions are multiple choice. All Reading and Writing questions use four-option multiple choice. In Math, approximately 75% of questions are four-option multiple choice and approximately 25% are student-produced response questions, where you enter the answer yourself.


### Can You Use a Calculator on All SAT Math Questions?


Yes. The Digital SAT allows calculator use throughout the entire Math section. The Bluebook testing application also includes a built-in Desmos calculator, and students may use an approved personal calculator if they prefer. The old separate “No Calculator” Math section no longer applies to the Digital SAT.
